title: Taking and learning from a practice exam
author: cm-strategy-author
summary: How to sit a Liminal practice exam under the conditions of the AP® Physics C: Mechanics Exam, mark your confidence as you go, write down the raw points you expect before opening the key, redo misses cold, score the multiple choice and the free-response rubrics honestly, and turn every lost point into a logged cause and a dated next task on this course's exam-preparation page.

blocks.text: A full practice exam costs three hours, and most of its value comes afterward, from what you change because of it. Taking form after form without that step mostly rehearses what you can already do. The cycle below sits the form on day 0, analyzes it within two days, and brings every missed item back within a week.

items: Sit the form under exam conditions: timed, with a calculator and the formula reference printed at the end of the student copy, and nothing else.
Mark each multiple-choice answer S, U or G in the margin as you go. When time is up, write down the raw points you expect for each section before you see the key.
Within one or two days, redo every miss and every item marked U or G cold, then read the key for the reasons, then score free response row by row with the rubrics.
Log every lost point with its unit, its cause, a next action on the exam-preparation page and a retry date.
On the next form, compare raw points by section, by unit and by question type, and compare each expectation with what you earned.

blocks.text: Take the whole form in one sitting when you can: 3 hours of working time, as on the exam. Concentration and pacing late in the sitting are part of what you are practising. When one long block is impossible, take Section I (85 minutes) and Section II (95 minutes) as two timed sittings a day or two apart, and never split a section. Two sittings still give honest raw points by section, but they cannot show how you work when tired, so take at least one form, ideally your last before the exam, in one sitting.

blocks.text: On the exam itself, delivery is hybrid digital: you answer multiple choice and read the free-response prompts in the Bluebook app, and you handwrite free-response answers in a paper booklet. Bluebook includes a Desmos scientific or graphing calculator, and you may also bring up to two approved handheld calculators. An equation sheet is supplied, printed for the exam room and also available in Bluebook. (College Board's exam and calculator-policy pages, checked 2026-10-22.) Liminal's practice exams append Liminal's own formula reference instead, which is arranged differently, so look over College Board's equation sheet from its exam page before the exam as well.

items: Print the student copy. Answer multiple choice on its answer sheet, keeping the margin for the marks described below, and handwrite free response in the space under each part, as you will in the paper booklet.
Use a timer you cannot pause, and stop when a section's time ends. If you want to finish an item afterward, use a different color; that work does not count toward the raw points.
Use the calculator you will use on the exam, in both sections.
Use the formula reference printed at the end of the student copy, and nothing else: no notes, textbook or phone. A form taken with notes open measures the notes.

Know Liminal's practice scoring before you begin. Each multiple-choice question is worth 1 raw point and nothing is taken off for a wrong choice, so Section I holds 42 raw points. Liminal scores the free-response types out of 10 (Mathematical Routines), 12 (Translation Between Representations), 10 (Experimental Design and Analysis) and 8 (Qualitative/Quantitative Translation), so Section II holds 40. Those point values are Liminal conventions; College Board's exam pages do not state them.

blocks.text: The Experimental Design and Analysis question is a paper investigation. Paper practice does not replace the hands-on lab work the AP® physics courses require.
Pausing the clock to look something up, or finishing a section with extra time, and then comparing those raw points with a form taken under the rules.
blocks.fix: Keep one set of conditions for every form. Then a change between forms means a change in you, not in the conditions.

blocks.text: In the margin of the answer sheet, beside each multiple-choice answer, write one letter.

head: Mark
Meaning
rows: You would bet on it: you worked it and checked it, or you know the fact.
You worked it but doubt a step, or you narrowed it to two choices.
You chose without a method that reached an answer.

blocks.text: Mark as you answer, not at the end. A mark written after you have seen later questions, or the key, records hindsight rather than confidence. The marks cost a second each and do two jobs later: they pick out the correct answers that still need a redo, and they show whether your sense of sure matches your results. In free response, write a small U beside any part where you doubt the principle, the setup or the justification.

Write the clock time in the margin after questions 14, 28 and 42 of Section I, and at the end of each free-response question. An even pace in Section I reaches question 14 at about 28 minutes and question 28 at about 57. Liminal's practice pace for Section II gives the four questions about 22, 28, 27 and 18 minutes, inside the suggested times printed on practice exam A. Circle the number of any item you skip to return to. These notes are what let you tell a time error from a knowledge error afterward; the guide on how the exam runs covers pacing in more detail.

When the last section ends, and before you open the key, write your expected raw points: Section I out of 42, and each free-response question out of its points. Students tend to stay overconfident from exam to exam, partly because they do not use their own past results (Foster et al. 2017). A written expectation, later set beside the result, is what lets you correct that.

sections.title: After: within one or two days

blocks.text: Do the analysis within a day or two, while you still remember why you chose what you chose. Hold every solution back until step 3.

items: Mark multiple choice from the key's letters alone, without reading rationales. Circle every wrong answer.

Redo cold. On a fresh page, untimed, with only the formula reference, rework every missed item and every item marked U or G, including the ones you got right. Start with the sure-but-wrong items. Add any free-response part you left unfinished or marked U.

Then open the key. For each redone item, read the rationale and the steps, and for a wrong choice read the note on the letter you picked, which names the error that produces it. Read for why each step is valid, not only for the answer.
Score free response with the rubrics, row by row, as described below.
Fill in the error log, and give every row a next action and a retry date.

blocks.text: Why this order. Making an error and then getting corrective feedback helps you learn, and errors made with high confidence are among the easiest to correct once the right answer is shown (Metcalfe 2017). So the sure-but-wrong items come first; they are also the ones you would otherwise never look at again. Feedback that explains why an answer is right helps more on new questions than feedback that only gives the answer (Butler et al. 2013), so read the steps, not just the letter. The cold redo comes before the key because it sorts your errors: what you fix alone, untimed, points to time, reading or a slip; what you cannot fix points to a concept, a principle choice or a calculus setup.
Spending half an hour on a cold redo of an item you cannot start.
blocks.fix: Cap a cold redo at about 5 minutes for a multiple-choice item and 10 minutes for a free-response part. If no principle has started to work by then, write down how far you got and open the key. Being unable to start is itself the diagnosis: a concept or a principle choice.

blocks.prompt: You start the cold redo of a form with a 75-minute block, the key still closed. Your list holds 9 missed multiple-choice items, 2 of them marked S; 5 correct items marked U or G; and 3 free-response parts, one unfinished and two marked U. (a) Under this guide's caps, what is the most time the list can take, and does it fit? (b) In what order do you take the list, and what happens to anything left when the block ends? (c) Twenty minutes in, you have spent 5 minutes on a missed item marked U, and no principle has started to work. What do you do, and what does that suggest about the item's cause?
blocks.hint: Cap each multiple-choice item at about 5 minutes and each free-response part at about 10.
blocks.answer: (a) Up to about 100 minutes: 14 multiple-choice items at about 5 minutes each and 3 free-response parts at about 10 minutes each, more than the 75-minute block. (b) The 2 sure-but-wrong items first, then the rest of the list. Anything left waits for a second sitting the next day, still within one or two days of the form and still before you open the key for it. (c) Stop at the cap: write down how far you got, open the key for that item, and move on. Being unable to start points to a concept or a principle choice, not to time or a slip.
steps: Multiple choice: 9 missed + 5 correct but marked U or G = 14 items, at about 5 minutes each = 70 minutes.
Free response: 3 parts at about 10 minutes each = 30 minutes. Together, about 100 minutes at the caps. Many items take less than their cap, so the list may still fit, but you cannot count on it.
Sure-but-wrong items come first: there your confidence and your result disagree most, and errors made with high confidence are among the easiest to correct once the right answer is shown.
Do not drop the correct U and G items to save time. A shaky or lucky answer will not reliably repeat, and the redo is how you find out which it was.

At the cap, the trap fix applies: note how far you got and open the key. If no principle started to work in 5 minutes, the gap is in the physics, so the log row's cause is a concept or a principle choice, and the cold redo has done its job.

blocks.text: Score free response honestly. The rubric awards points for what is on the page, so score it the way a stranger would.

items: Score each rubric row on its own. A row you would have earned if you had written something is a row lost.

A starting-principle row needs the principle in symbols for this system: ΣF = ma with the actual forces, an energy or momentum statement with its terms. A line of numbers does not show which law produced it.
A derivation row needs the final expression in the symbols the part allows. An expression that still contains a tension or an acceleration not on the list is unfinished.
An answer row needs the unit, and a sensible number of significant figures. Keys accept ±1 in the last digit.
A justification row needs the principle and the reason its condition holds here, not only the conclusion.
A free-body diagram row needs forces only, each drawn from the dot and labeled; components or a net-force arrow drawn among the forces lose it where the rubric says so.
Check every equals sign. Two different quantities chained together with = is a false statement, and Liminal's rubrics can withhold a row for it even when the number is right.
Score one answer per part. If two different answers to a part are left standing, credit neither.
Where a rubric row credits work that is consistent with an earlier wrong answer, apply it; where it does not, do not invent the credit.

When you cannot tell whether a row is earned, do not award it, and log why. If you can, trade a question with a classmate and score each other's; a second reader shows how generous you are with yourself.

blocks.prompt: A free-response part reads: "A 0.50 kg block at rest on a level, frictionless track is pushed by a horizontal force F(x) = 8.0 − 2.0x, in newtons with x in meters, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3.0 m. Calculate the block's speed at x = 3.0 m." Its rubric: 1 point for applying the work–energy theorem with the work written as a definite integral, ½mv^2 = ∫ from 0 to 3.0 of F(x) dx; 1 point for evaluating the integral correctly, 15 (J); 1 point for v = 7.7 m/s, with units. A student wrote: "∫ F dx = 8.0x − x^2 = 15, so ½(0.50)v^2 = 15 and v = 7.7". Score it row by row, and name the cause of each lost point.
blocks.hint: Check each rubric row against exactly what is written, then work the problem yourself.
blocks.answer: 1 of 3 points. No first point: the integral has no limits, and "8.0x − x^2 = 15" sets a function equal to a number. The second point is earned: the integral's value, 15, is correct. No third point: the speed has no unit. Two log rows, both communication: a setup without limits written as a false equality, and an answer without a unit.
steps: Setup: "∫ F dx" without limits is not the work from 0 to 3.0 m, and 8.0x − x^2 equals 15 only at x = 3.0 m (or 5.0 m), so the row "a definite integral" is not met by what is written.
Value: ∫ from 0 to 3.0 of (8.0 − 2.0x) dx = 24 − 9.0 = 15 J. The rubric accepts 15, so that point is earned.

Answer: ½(0.50 kg)v^2 = 15 J gives v^2 = 60 m^2/s^2 and v = 7.75 m/s, which rounds to 7.7 m/s with the givens' two significant figures, keys accepting ±1 in the last digit. The student's 7.7 is right but has no unit, so the answer row is lost.
Total: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1 of 3.
Rewrite: W = ∫ from 0 to 3.0 of (8.0 − 2.0x) dx = 15 J, and ½(0.50 kg)v^2 = 15 J, so v = 7.7 m/s.

rows: You did not know or misremembered the physics: mechanical energy conserved with friction acting, μ_sN used as the actual static friction, gravity treated as changing a spring's period.
You still cannot do it alone, and the key's reason is new to you.
You know the laws but applied the wrong one, or chose a system that made a needed force internal or an internal force external.
Once you know which principle and system to use, you finish quickly.
The wrong element, limits or variable of integration, a dropped constant, or constant-acceleration relations used with a varying force.
Writing the small element (dm, dW, dJ) first lets you finish, or you stall again at the same step.
A graph or diagram misread: height for slope, a component for a magnitude, sine and cosine swapped, a free-body diagram with a force missing or added.
You get it right once you reread the axes or redraw the diagram.
Right principle and setup, slip in carrying it out: a sign in algebra, a dropped square, degree mode, a value rounded too early.
You get it right on the redo, or find the slip by checking your own steps.
A unit missing or wrong, or a direction convention changed partway through.
Your number is right but its unit or sign is not, or the sign flips where you switched conventions.
You answered a different question: speed for velocity, one object for the system, the force on A for the force by A, a value at the wrong instant.
You get it right as soon as you reread the last line of the prompt.
The physics was right but the page did not earn the row: no starting principle, a condition left unnamed, a false equality, symbols outside the allowed list.
Your answer matches the key, but a rubric row is not met by what you wrote.
You did not reach the item, or rushed it; your clock notes show the section ran out.
You solve it untimed at a reasonable pace.

blocks.text: When two causes fit one point, log the earlier link in the chain: a concept gap that led to a slow, confused attempt is a concept error, not a time error. When a free-response part lost points for two separate reasons, give it two rows. The categories fail when you honestly cannot tell which applies. Then pick the one with the more useful next action, and let the retry confirm or correct it.

A log changes nothing by itself. In one classroom study, filling in reflection forms after exams, with nothing following from them, did not improve students' later grades or their judgment of their own learning (Soicher & Gurung 2017). What helps is the task the reflection leads to, so every row gets a specific task on this course's exam-preparation page and a date.

blocks.text: Read the log two ways. The same cause in several units points to a skill, such as setting up integrals or stating a direction, to practise on fresh items across units. Lost points clustered in one unit point to content, which that unit's review addresses. Free-response points also sort by question type: each form has one question of each type, so the type with the largest share of its points lost gets the next two questions of its workshop set.

Put every missed item back on the calendar 2 to 7 days later, and redo it cold again. A retry the next day mostly tests short-term memory; one left for weeks may not happen before the next form. On the retry, also do one fresh item of the same kind from a unit review or a mixed set, because a repeated item can turn into remembering its answer rather than solving it.

Work first on the cause that cost the most points, but not only on that one. This rule fails when the biggest cause is time: running out of time often comes from slow setups earlier in the section, so read your clock notes and the items around the gap before you treat it as a pacing problem.

blocks.prompt: A multiple-choice item gave a force F(x) that pushes a cart from rest along a frictionless track and asked for the cart's speed at a given x. You marked it S. You had evaluated F at the final position, used a = F/m and then v^2 = 2ax, and your choice was wrong. In the cold redo you tried to integrate dv/dt and stalled, because the force was given in terms of x. When the key's first step said W = ∫ F dx = ΔK, you finished in two minutes. Name the cause, a next task and a retry window.
blocks.hint: Ask what the key's first line gave you that you did not already have.
blocks.answer: Principle or system choice: the work–energy theorem was the principle to use. Next task: a timed mixed set, writing the system and the principle before solving each item, and this item again, cold, between day 2 and day 7.
steps: Once you were told the principle, you carried it out correctly and quickly, so the integration itself is sound.

A force given in terms of position, with a speed asked and no time, points to W = ∫ F dx. You know that theorem but did not choose it here: a principle-choice error, not a concept or calculus-setup error.

Treating a varying force as constant is also listed under calculus setup, but the cold redo decides between the two: once the key named the theorem you finished at once, so the earlier link in the chain was the choice of principle, and that is the cause to log.
Choosing a principle is trained by mixed practice, where deciding what applies is part of every item; writing the system and principle first makes the choice visible.
Using a = F/m with the final force treated a changing force as constant, which is the trap that choice was built on.
The item was marked S, so it belonged at the front of the redo list.

blocks.prompt: A free-response part asked whether the mechanical energy of a block–spring system is constant as the block oscillates on a level, frictionless surface. You wrote "Yes, energy is conserved" and earned 0 of the 1 justification point. In the cold redo, without the key, you wrote at once that only the spring does work on the block, because the surface is frictionless and gravity and the normal force are perpendicular to the motion. Classify the error, give a next task, and say what result of the redo would have changed the classification.
blocks.hint: The cold redo is the test between two causes. What did it show you already knew?
blocks.answer: Communication: you knew the reason but did not write it. Next task: the justification section of the free-response writing guide, then rewrite this answer so it names the condition. If the redo had again said only that energy is always conserved, the cause would be concept, since total energy and mechanical energy are different claims, and the next task would be the rules on mechanical energy in the unit 3 review.
steps: "Energy is conserved" is true of total energy in every case, so it does not show why mechanical energy is constant here.
The justification point needs the condition: only conservative forces do work on the system.
You supplied that condition unaided in the cold redo, so the knowledge was there and the written answer was the problem.

Rewritten answer: Yes. The surface is frictionless, and gravity and the normal force are perpendicular to the motion, so only the spring does work on the block, and the system's mechanical energy is constant.

blocks.prompt: After practice exam B your log shows these lost points. Unit 2: 4 (3 calculus setup with velocity-dependent forces, 1 reading the question). Unit 3: 3 (2 calculus setup with work integrals, 1 algebra). Unit 5: 3 (2 calculus setup with rotational inertia, 1 concept). Unit 6: 4 (all concept: angular momentum about a pivot, in 3 multiple-choice items and 1 free-response part). Other units: 4, with scattered causes. Name the two next tasks that address the most points, with where each is on the exam-preparation page.
blocks.hint: Total the points by cause across units, and by unit for each cause. Which cause recurs across units, and which unit has one cause?
blocks.answer: First, calculus setup, which recurs across units 2, 3 and 5 for 7 points, so treat it as a skill: the calculus-methods guide and its checks, then setup retry items from the unit 2, 3 and 5 reviews on different days. Second, unit 6's concept errors, 4 points clustered in one unit, so treat them as content: the unit 6 review's rules and worked example on angular momentum, then its checks, then the missed items again, cold.
steps: Calculus setup: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 points across three units, the largest cause.
Concept in unit 6: 4 points, all in one unit and one idea.
One cause spread over several units points to a skill practised on fresh items across units; one unit with one cause points to that unit's content.
The remaining points, 1 reading, 1 algebra, 1 concept in unit 5 and the scattered 4, each get their own log row and retry date, but not the first two tasks.

blocks.text: From the second form on, set the new raw points beside the old ones by section, by unit and by question type, and set each expectation beside its result. Liminal's practice exams give every unit the same number of multiple-choice questions on every form (5 each for units 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7; 9 for unit 2; 8 for unit 3), so those unit counts compare directly. Free response places each question type on different units from form to form, so compare free-response points by type, not by unit.

blocks.text: Calibration. Subtract each result from its expectation. A gap that shrinks across forms suggests your judgment of your own work is improving, which matters on the exam itself when you decide which answers to check. Do the same with your S marks: if more than about 1 in 10 sure answers are wrong, check an answer before you mark it S. With only a handful of S marks that fraction jumps with a single item, so read it over two forms.

Read the comparison for patterns, not single numbers. Forms differ in difficulty, and a unit with five multiple-choice questions can move two points on one lucky guess and one slip. Trust a change that appears on two forms and agrees with the causes in your log. Do not retake the same form to compare, since you will partly remember it.
The shares of exam score in the format table describe the real exam. They are not a formula to apply to Liminal's raw points, which stay raw, by section, as practice evidence.

blocks.prompt: Use the example comparison above. (a) Combine the two forms' sure answers. By this guide's rule for S marks, should you still check an answer before marking it S? Why combine the forms rather than read form B alone? (b) Your Section II expectation was 27 on both forms, and its gap to the result shrank from 6 points to 2. Does that show that your judgment of your own free-response work improved? (c) Which free-response type should get the next two questions of its workshop set?
blocks.hint: For (a), add the wrong sure answers and the sure answers over both forms. For (b), ask which number moved. For (c), compare the share of each type's points lost on form B, not the raw number lost.
blocks.answer: (a) Yes: 8 of your 50 sure answers were wrong, 16%, well above about 1 in 10. Form B alone, 3 of 26 or about 12%, sits close to the bar, and one item more or less would move it across, so read the fraction over both forms. (b) Not by itself: the expectation stayed at 27, and the gap shrank because the result rose from 21 to 25. Better judgment would show as an expectation that moves with the result. (c) Qualitative/Quantitative Translation: it lost 4 of 8 points, half its points, the largest share of any type, on both forms.
steps: Wrong sure answers: 24 − 19 = 5 on form A and 26 − 23 = 3 on form B, so 8 of 24 + 26 = 50, or 16%.

Form B alone: 3 of 26 ≈ 12%. One more right sure answer would make it 2 of 26 ≈ 8%, under the bar; one more wrong one, 4 of 26 ≈ 15%. With few S marks a single item moves the fraction, which is why the guide reads it over two forms.

Section II gaps: 27 − 21 = 6 on form A and 27 − 25 = 2 on form B. The expectation did not change; the result did. A shrinking gap suggests better calibration only when the expectation itself tracks the result, for example by falling on a form where the result falls.

Share lost on form B: Mathematical Routines 3 of 10 (30%), Translation Between Representations 4 of 12 (33%), Experimental Design and Analysis 4 of 10 (40%), Qualitative/Quantitative Translation 4 of 8 (50%). Form A's share for that type was also 4 of 8, so the pattern held on two forms.

blocks.text: Write each log entry, and any comment on a classmate's work, about the physics, not about the person. Feedback that turns attention toward the self rather than the task often fails to help and sometimes hurts (Kluger & DeNisi 1996). A cause that names a step can be fixed; a verdict about a person cannot.

blocks.prompt: The cause column for a missed collision item
blocks.text: Principle choice: I conserved linear momentum for the ball and the rod on a pivot. The pivot pushes on the rod during the impact, so only angular momentum about the pivot is constant.
Log entries such as "bad at rotation" or "careless again".
blocks.fix: Name the step that failed and the correct step. "Careless" is not a cause: if it keeps happening, it is a procedure to retry or a check to add, and the log should say which.
